keyVerseText: Therefore the anger of the LORD was hot against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Chushanrishathaim king of Mesopotamia: and the children of Israel served Chushanrishathaim eight years. Mesopotamia: Heb. Aramnaharaim
rootMeaning: The term כּוּשַׁן רִשְׁעָתַיִם (Kûwshan Rishʻâthayim) is composed of two parts: כּוּשָׁן (Kûwshân), which is related to a place name possibly in Arabia or Mesopotamia and carries the idea of "their blackness," and רִשְׁעָתַיִם (Rishʻâthayim), the dual form of רִשְׁעָה meaning "wickedness." Together, the name literally means "Cushan of double wickedness" or "twice-wicked Cushan," emphasizing a heightened degree of moral corruption or evil. This etymology enriches the understanding beyond a simple proper name by highlighting the character or reputation associated with this figure.
usageInScripture: The name כּוּשַׁן רִשְׁעָתַיִם occurs four times in the book of Judges, consistently translated as Chushanrishathaim. It refers exclusively to a Mesopotamian king who oppressed Israel, illustrating a specific historical and theological role rather than a general or symbolic term. The consistent use of the full name underlines the severity of his oppression and the moral judgment implied in the name itself.
theologicalSignificance: The designation "twice-wicked Cushan" reveals how Scripture uses names to convey spiritual realities, portraying this king not only as a political adversary but as a symbol of intensified evil opposing God's people. His oppression of Israel reflects God's righteous judgment on the nation when they turn away from Him, demonstrating divine sovereignty over history. For the Christian faith, this reminds believers of the consequences of sin and the necessity of deliverance through God's appointed means, prefiguring Christ as the ultimate deliverer from bondage to evil. The name's dual wickedness underscores the depth of human rebellion that only God's grace can overcome.
keyVerseReflection: Judges 3:8 states, "Therefore the anger of the LORD was hot against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Chushanrishathaim king of Mesopotamia," emphasizing that Israel's suffering under this king was a direct consequence of divine judgment. The name Chushanrishathaim, meaning "twice-wicked Cushan," heightens the sense of the severity and moral darkness of the oppression Israel endured. This deepens the reader's understanding of the seriousness of Israel's sin and the formidable nature of the adversary God allowed to discipline them.
